stimulus.text:
“The first question that presents itself on the subject is, whether a confederated government be the best for the United States or not? Or in other words, whether the thirteen United States should be reduced to one great republic, governed by one legislature, and under the direction of one executive and judicial; or whether they should continue thirteen confederated republics, under the direction and controul of a supreme federal head for certain defined national purposes only? . . . This government is to possess absolute and uncontroulable power, legislative, executive and judicial, with respect to every object to which it extends, for by the last clause of section 8th, article 1st, it is declared ‘that the Congress shall have power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers.’”

—Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787
stimulus.source_note: Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

stem: Why does Brutus quote the Necessary and Proper Clause in this passage?

options.text: To show that the president could veto any law he disliked
options.misconception: The clause is about Congress's power to make laws, not about a presidential veto.

options.text: To show that Congress would be strictly limited to the powers listed
options.misconception: Brutus reads the clause as giving Congress absolute and uncontrollable power, not as a strict limit.

options.text: To show that the states could overrule any law Congress passed
options.misconception: Brutus says state laws are nullified where they clash with the Constitution, not that states can overrule Congress.

options.text: To show Congress could stretch its powers beyond the listed ones

rationales.A: The clause concerns Congress's lawmaking power; no presidential veto is mentioned.
rationales.B: Brutus reads the clause as expanding Congress's power, not as limiting it to a strict list.
rationales.C: Background: elsewhere in the essay Brutus says state constitutions and laws are nullified where they conflict, the opposite of states overruling Congress.
rationales.D: Brutus quotes the clause to prove his charge: Congress may make all laws necessary and proper for carrying its powers into execution, so its power is absolute and uncontrollable with respect to every object it reaches.
rationales.general:
1. Brutus's charge is that the new government will hold absolute and uncontrollable power.
2. His evidence is the clause itself: Congress may make all laws necessary and proper.
3. He reads those words as letting Congress decide the reach of its own power.
4. Background: the Supremacy Clause then makes federal law override state law where they clash.
Remember: a quotation in an argument is evidence, so ask what charge it is meant to prove.
